title: ECMAScript Standardization, TC39 and Modern JavaScript Evolution
learningObjectives: Define ECMAScript as the standardized core language specification associated with JavaScript.
Explain why standardization helps different JavaScript engines implement compatible language behaviour.
Identify Ecma International and Technical Committee 39 (TC39) as key parts of ECMAScript standardization.
Describe the adoption of the first ECMA-262 edition in 1997.
Explain at a high level how language proposals are discussed, reviewed, tested and incorporated into editions of the standard.
Distinguish the ECMAScript language specification from browser Web APIs such as the DOM and Fetch.
Explain why modern JavaScript features are introduced through an ongoing standards process rather than one permanent final version.
Recognize that JavaScript engines may implement features at different times and that compatibility testing remains necessary.
Explain the role of transpilers and build tools when a project targets environments without support for a desired syntax feature.
Use MDN, TC39 and Ecma documentation to verify language features and their current support.
Distinguish JavaScript language features from libraries, frameworks and host runtime APIs.
Apply standards-aware reasoning when selecting syntax for a browser or server project.

understand.concept: ECMAScript is the standardized core language specification associated with JavaScript. Ecma International publishes the ECMA-262 specification, and Technical Committee 39 (TC39) is involved in its development. Standardization helps independent JavaScript engines implement compatible language behaviour. The language continues to evolve through proposals, review, testing and new editions. Browser APIs such as the DOM are separate Web platform specifications, not part of the ECMAScript language itself.
understand.whyItMatters: Knowing the standardization model helps developers distinguish a language feature from a browser API, a library or a framework. It also encourages checking implementation support before using newer syntax in a project that must work across particular browsers or runtimes.
understand.analogy: A programming language standard is like a shared technical rulebook that multiple engine teams use so programs behave consistently across implementations.
understand.analogyLimit: A standard does not force every engine to ship a feature at the same moment. Implementations, tests, host APIs and developer tooling evolve on their own schedules, so compatibility must still be checked.
understand.history: The first edition of ECMA-262 was adopted in June 1997. The name ECMAScript was selected for the standardized language specification, while JavaScript remained the widely used name. Modern editions are published through an ongoing standards process, and feature development is coordinated through TC39 proposals and consensus.

explain.narrative:
JavaScript became widely used across browsers, so independent implementations needed a shared description of the language. Ecma International adopted the first edition of ECMA-262 in June 1997. The standardized language was named ECMAScript, while JavaScript remained the familiar name used by developers and browser vendors.

TC39 works on ECMAScript language development. New ideas are discussed as proposals, refined through review and testing, and considered for inclusion in the standard. This process helps the language evolve while preserving compatibility with existing programs. Modern JavaScript is not frozen at an old label such as ES5 or ES6; new editions and features continue to appear.

Separate the language standard from the host platform. ECMAScript defines core language behaviour such as expressions, functions, objects, modules and promises. A browser provides APIs such as document, fetch, localStorage and event listeners. A server runtime may provide file-system, process and networking APIs. A JavaScript program can use both language features and host APIs, but they come from different specifications.

Engine support may differ for newer features. Before using a feature, check the standard, implementation support and the project's target environment. A transpiler or build tool can transform some newer syntax into a form supported by older environments, but it cannot automatically polyfill every missing host API or runtime behaviour. Test the built output in the environments your users actually use.

examples.explanation: The example uses core language features. The DOM insertion is a browser API provided by the host environment.
examples.expectedOutput: A browser page displays or updates text using JavaScript.

examples.title: Language standard and host API layers
examples.code:
ECMA-262:
- variables, functions, objects, promises, modules

Browser Web APIs:
- document, events, Fetch, localStorage

Server runtime APIs:
- process, file system, server networking
examples.explanation: ECMAScript does not define every host API. A JavaScript application combines core language features with capabilities supplied by its runtime.
examples.expectedOutput: You can classify common features by the specification or host that provides them.

examples.title: Check a feature before adopting it
examples.code:
1. Find the feature in ECMAScript documentation.
2. Check engine support for target browsers/runtimes.
3. Decide whether a build transform is needed.
4. Check whether a missing API needs a polyfill or alternative.
5. Run tests in the supported environments.
examples.explanation: Syntax transforms and API polyfills solve different problems. A transpiler can rewrite syntax, but it does not guarantee that a missing browser API exists.
examples.expectedOutput: A compatibility decision that matches the project's supported environments.

examples.title: Standard language features and libraries are different
examples.code:
Array.prototype.map(...)  // standard language/runtime API
React components          // library ecosystem
fetch(...)                 // host API in browsers and many runtimes
import ...                 // ECMAScript module syntax
examples.explanation: A framework or library may use standard language features and host APIs, but it is not itself part of ECMA-262.
examples.expectedOutput: You can identify the correct documentation source for a feature.

practise.guidedTask: Choose one JavaScript feature and determine whether it is part of ECMAScript, a browser API or a third-party library. Check its standard documentation and target-runtime support. Explain whether a transpiler, polyfill or different implementation is required.
practise.independentTask: Write a short compatibility plan for a JavaScript feature used in a browser project. Include the ECMAScript feature, target browser/runtime support, build transformation needs, API polyfill needs and tests. Explain why a syntax transform cannot supply every missing host API.
hints: ECMAScript defines the core language; JavaScript is the common name used by developers.
TC39 works on ECMAScript language development.
The first ECMA-262 edition was adopted in 1997.
The DOM and Fetch are Web APIs, not core ECMAScript features.
Transpilers transform syntax; polyfills may provide missing APIs, where possible.
Always check the project's actual target environments.

practice.starterCode:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>ECMAScript standardization and modern evolution</title></head><body>
<script>const values=[1,2,3];const doubled=values.map(value=>value*2);document.body.insertAdjacentText('beforeend',doubled.join(', '));</script>
</body></html>
practice.resetCode:

<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><title>ECMAScript standardization and modern evolution</title></head><body>

</body></html>

questions.prompt: Which standard specifies the core JavaScript language?
questions.explanation: ECMAScript defines the core JavaScript language.

questions.prompt: What should you identify before using a JavaScript API?
questions.explanation: Available APIs depend on whether code runs in a browser, server runtime, or another host.
ECMA-262 defines the ECMAScript language used by JavaScript implementations.

questions.prompt: Which organization is associated with ECMAScript language proposals?
questions.explanation: Technical Committee 39 works on ECMAScript language development.

questions.prompt: Can a transpiler automatically provide every missing browser API?
options: No. Syntax transformation and API availability are different problems.
Yes, it creates every browser capability automatically.
Yes, it replaces the browser engine.
questions.answer: No. Syntax transformation and API availability are different problems.
questions.explanation: A transpiler can transform syntax, but missing runtime APIs may require a polyfill or alternative and cannot always be reproduced.
